p.x:
For my birthday, my family took me to a small Thai restaurant near the river. The waiter was very friendly. He gave us a table by the window and brought us glasses of cold water.
We ordered lots of dishes to share. First, we had a spicy papaya salad and a big bowl of tom yum soup. The soup was sweet and sour, and it had fresh prawns in it. Then the waiter brought plates of fried noodles with a special peanut sauce. My little brother couldn't use chopsticks, so he asked for a fork and a knife.
At the end of the meal, the chef came out of the kitchen and sang "Happy Birthday" with all the staff. When the bill came, my father paid by card and left a big tip. It was the best birthday dinner ever!

Ning has worked at a busy restaurant in Bangkok for three years. She started as a cashier, taking payments at the front counter, but now she is a supervisor. "Restaurant work is hard," she says. "You're on your feet all day, and customers can be very demanding."
Lunchtime is the busiest period. The restaurant serves a buffet for office workers, and at the same time, delivery riders arrive every few minutes to collect takeaway orders. Ning's job is to make sure everything runs smoothly. She checks that tables are cleaned quickly, that napkins and sauces are refilled, and that starters arrive before main courses.
The restaurant's menu has changed a lot. "Ten years ago, nobody asked about vegan food," Ning says. "Now we have five vegan dishes, and they're very popular." The chef has also reduced the amount of oil, because many customers complained that some dishes were too greasy.
What does Ning like most about her job? "When customers say the food was tasty and the service was excellent, it makes all the hard work worth it."

p.t: The Rise of Thai Fine Dining
p.x:
Not long ago, the idea of paying 5,000 baht for a Thai meal would have seemed absurd. Thai food was associated with cheap, delicious street stalls, not with gourmet restaurants. Today, however, Bangkok has several restaurants with international awards, and chefs are reinventing traditional recipes for a more demanding palate.
These restaurants offer far more than food. Diners pay for the ambience: elegant lighting, attentive staff and beautiful tableware, from hand-made plates to silver cutlery. Many places serve a tasting menu of ten or more small courses, often including the chef's signature dish. A complimentary glass of fruit juice or a small surprise course between dishes adds to the sense of luxury. Some restaurants offer carefully chosen beverage pairings, matching each course with a different drink.
Fine-dining chefs often emphasise seasonal ingredients from small local farms, and kitchens follow strict hygiene standards. Some also cater for guests with special diets, creating entire menus without meat or gluten.
Critics argue that fine dining is an expensive way to indulge, and that the best Thai food is still found on the street. Supporters reply that the two worlds can exist side by side, and that the global attention helps promote Thai cuisine as a whole.
